A vector is a mathematical object that is used to represent quantities that have both direction and magnitude. We can think of a vector as a "directed line segment".

Content:
For example, consider a ship that travels [MATH: 15\:\textrm{km}] due east. In the diagram below, the ship starts at the point [MATH: A] and ends at the point [MATH: B.] This information can be represented as a vector, a directed line segment that starts at [MATH: A] and points to [MATH: B,] as follows:

The vector itself represents the displacement of the ship. The magnitude (length) of the vector represents the total distance traveled, and the direction of the vector gives the direction of travel.

Content:

Two vectors are equal if and only if they lie on parallel lines and have both the same magnitude and the same direction.

The vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{e}] are parallel and have the same direction and magnitude, hence [MATH: \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{e}.] Similarly, [MATH: \mathbf{b}] and [MATH: \mathbf{d}] are parallel and have the same direction and magnitude, hence [MATH: \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{d}.]

On the other hand, [MATH: \mathbf{a} eq \mathbf{b}], [MATH: \mathbf{a} eq \mathbf{c}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b} eq \mathbf{c}] because they are not parallel.

Therefore, we get [MATH: \mathbf{a}=\mathbf{e}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}=\mathbf{d}] only.
